DEPARTMENT 6 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 24PSCV04481    Hearing Date: August 25, 2026    Dept: 6

CASE NAME:  Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club v. Vicente Reyes Vargas 

Plaintiff Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club’s Motion to Enforce Settlement Agreement and Enter Judgment Against Defendant Vicente Reyes Vargas 

TENTATIVE RULING 

The Court GRANTS Plaintiff Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club’s Motion to Enforce Settlement Agreement and Enter Judgment Against Defendant Vicente Reyes Vargas. The Court directs Plaintiff to submit the proposed Judgment as a separate document, prior to the hearing, for the Court to sign. 

            Plaintiff is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order. 

BACKGROUND 

This is a subrogation action. On December 30, 2024, plaintiff Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club (Plaintiff) filed this action against defendant Vicente Reyes Vargas (Defendant) and Does 1 through 10, alleging one cause of action for subrogation. 

On February 6, 2026, Plaintiff dismissed this action without prejudice and with the Court retaining jurisdiction under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6. 

On July 21, 2026, Plaintiff moved to enforce settlement agreement and enter judgment against Defendant. Defendant did not oppose the Motion. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

“If parties to pending litigation stipulate, in a writing signed by the parties outside of the presence of the court or orally before the court, for settlement of the case, or part thereof, the court, upon motion, may enter judgment pursuant to the terms of the settlement. If the parties to the settlement agreement or their counsel stipulate in writing or orally before the court, the court may dismiss the case as to the settling parties without prejudice and retain jurisdiction over the parties to enforce the settlement until performance in full of the terms of the settlement.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 664.6, subd. (a).) 

“A party may file a motion or other document pertaining to the settlement, including an application for determination of good faith settlement, a motion for the reduction or determination of a lien, a petition related to the compromise of the claim of a minor or person with a disability, or, if the terms of a settlement are not performed, a motion based upon such terms. Responsive filings and related documents may also be filed.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 664.6, subd. (f)(1).) 

PRELIMINARY ISSUES 

The Court notes that Plaintiff’s Motion quotes an outdated version of Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6. (Motion, 4:21-25.) The Court admonishes Plaintiff to properly quote the law going forward. 

DISCUSSION 

Plaintiff moves under Code of Civil Procedure sections 187 and 664.6 to enforce the parties’ December 23, 2025 Stipulation for Entry of Judgment and Installment Payments (the Stipulation) and to enter judgment against Defendant. Plaintiff states that the Stipulation stayed judgment while Defendant paid $3,860.74 through his insurance carrier plus monthly installments of $75.00 totaling $11,360.74, and that paragraph 9 of the Stipulation reserves the Court's jurisdiction to enforce judgment under section 664.6. Plaintiff contends Defendant has defaulted, asserting that the carrier paid the initial $3,860.74 but Defendant thereafter paid only $225.00, with no payment received after March 14, 2026. Relying on paragraphs 1 and 5 through 8 of the Stipulation, under which Defendant acknowledged that the underlying amount is the actual amount due and owing and not a penalty, and agreed that a declaration of default is conclusive proof of the default and amount owed, Plaintiff requests entry of judgment for the principal sum of $47,017.17, plus $3,619.68 in interest at 5% per annum from December 30, 2024, through July 15, 2026, less a $4,085.74 credit for payments received, plus $534.00 in costs, for a total of $47,085.11, with interest accruing at $6.44 per day. 

The Court finds Plaintiff’s Motion persuasive. The Court retained jurisdiction to enforce the Stipulation under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6 and paragraph 9 of the Stipulation expressly provides for the Court’s continuing jurisdiction under section 664.6. (Request for Dismissal (2/6/26); Tapper Decl., Ex. A, ¶ 9.) The Stipulation provides that Defendant was to make monthly installment payments totaling $11,360.74 as a negotiated settlement amount and that Plaintiff could obtain entry of judgment against Defendant in the amount of $47,017.17 plus interest from December 30, 2024, and court costs, less credit for all payments made before default, if Defendant failed to make the agreed upon installment payments. (Tapper Decl., Ex. A, ¶¶ 1-5; Creditors Adjustment Bureau, Inc. v. Imani (2022) 82 Cal.App.5th 131, 135 [stipulation for entry of judgment on full amount not a penalty where defendant acknowledged the full amount due].) Plaintiff’s evidence shows that Defendant stopped making payments after March 14, 2026. (Tapper Decl., ¶ 4.) Plaintiff is therefore entitled to entry of judgment under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6. The Court further finds Plaintiff’s prejudgment interest calculation correct. Plaintiff did not itemize its court costs, but the Court assumes these are correct given Defendant’s lack of opposition. (D.I. Chadbourne, Inc. v. Superior Court (1964) 60 Cal.2d 723, 728, fn. 4 [where nonmoving party fails to oppose a ground for a motion, “it is assumed that [nonmoving party] concedes” that ground].)

Based on the foregoing, the Court GRANTS the Motion. The Court will sign the separately lodged proposed judgment.

CONCLUSION 

The Court GRANTS Plaintiff Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club’s Motion to Enforce Settlement Agreement and Enter Judgment Against Defendant Vicente Reyes Vargas. The Court directs Plaintiff to submit the proposed Judgment as a separate document, prior to the hearing, for the Court to sign. 

Plaintiff is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order.

Case Number: 25PSCV03080    Hearing Date: August 25, 2026    Dept: 6

CASE NAME:  City of Glendora v. Tong Zhou, et al. 

March 2026 Monthly Accounting of Receivership Income, Expenses, and Interim Fees 

TENTATIVE RULING 

The Court APPROVES Receiver’s March 2026 report in the amount of $37,153.45. 

             Receiver is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order. 

BACKGROUND 

This is a nuisance case. On August 25, 2025, plaintiff City of Glendora (Plaintiff) filed this action against defendants Tong Zhou (Zhou), Ying Xia (Xia) (collectively, Defendants) and Does 1 through 20, alleging causes of action for public nuisance per se, public nuisance, violation of state housing law – receivership, and declaration/injunctive relief. 

On February 18, 2026, the Court approved Plaintiff’s motion for appointment of receiver and appointed California Receivership Group, Inc. (Receiver) as receiver over the subject property. 

 On April 30, 2026, Receiver filed the March 2026 monthly accounting of receivership income, expenses, and interim fees. On May 8, 2026, Plaintiff filed objections.

LEGAL STANDARD 

(a) Content of reports 

The receiver must provide monthly reports to the parties and, if requested, to nonparty client lien holders. These reports must include: 

(1) A narrative report of events; 

(2) A financial report; and 

(3) A statement of all fees paid to the receiver, employees, and professionals showing: 

(A) Itemized services; 

(B) A breakdown of the services by 1/10 hour increments; 

(C) If the fees are hourly, the hourly fees; and 

(D) If the fees are on another basis, that basis. 

(b) Reports not to be filed 

The monthly reports are not to be filed with the court unless the court so orders. 

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1182.) 

            (a) Interim fees 

Interim fees are subject to final review and approval by the court. The court retains jurisdiction to award a greater or lesser amount as the full, fair, and final value of the services received. 

(b) Objections to interim accounts and reports 

Unless good cause is shown, objections to a receiver's interim report and accounting must be made within 10 days of notice of the report and accounting, must be specific, and must be delivered to the receiver and all parties entitled to service of the interim report and accounting. 

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1183.) 

PRELIMINARY ISSUE 

            Financial account information is supposed to be redacted. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 1.201, subd. (a)(2).) Receiver failed to redact a bank account number. (March 2026 Report, p. 62 of pdf.) The Court admonishes Receiver to comply with the California Rules of Court going forward. 

DISCUSSION 

Receiver’s March 2026 report indicates having incurred $41,617.75 in receivership fees. Receiver states that total unpaid receivership fees and unpaid advances as of this reporting period are $41,617.75 and $0.00, respectively. Receiver sets forth details regarding rehabilitation work performed on the subject property through the month of March 2026. 

The Court has reviewed the March 2026 report and finds the $41,617.75 in receivership fees excessive. The Court notes approximately 14 timekeepers involved in this matter. (See March 2026 Report, pp. 65-98 of pdf.) While the Court understands and appreciates that multiple people are necessary for the significant demands involved in rehabilitating a property, 14 people is excessive. Of particular note is the extensive amount of minor billing entries from each of these timekeepers in the amounts of 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 hours throughout the March 2026 report. (See March 2026 Report, pp. 65-98.) The Court also notes that many of these charges contain block billing. (Heritage Pac. Fin., LLC v. Monroy (2013) 215 Cal.App.4th 972, 1010, internal citation omitted, “[t]rial courts retain discretion to penalize block billing when the practice prevents them from discerning which tasks are compensable and which are not…”) Additionally, the March 2026 report includes a 2/23/2026 entry from Erick Traschikoff in the amount of $18.50, which should not have been included and will be deducted. (March 2026 Report, p. 80 of pdf.) 

The Court also notes that much of Receiver’s billing entries are for administrative tasks, such as internal coordination, recurring meetings, bookkeeping/accounting, and processing credit card charges, among other things. The Court will therefore deduct $4,107.90 as follows:

The Court then notes that Receiver appears to have already paid itself for February 2026, notwithstanding the Court’s disapproval of the initial February 2026 report. (See Minute Order (4/27/26).) The March 2026 report includes the billing for the initial February 2026 report. (See March 2026 Report, pp. 9-50 of pdf.) The fees for the initial February 2026 report amount to $31,207.70. (See March 2026 Report, pp. 9-10, 14-19, 27-45.) The March 2026 report also shows multiple checks having been paid to Mark Adams, Receiver’s president, on March 15, 2026, totaling $31,207.70. (March 2026 Report, pp. 7-8 of pdf.) This was improper, as the Court had not yet approved those fees. (See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1183, subd. (a).) 

The Court further notes other improper charges, such as photocopying charges in the amounts of $20.83 and $7.71, and $85.80 for transferring funds to pay receivership fees or transferring funds from the trust account to the receivership account. (March 2026 Report, pp. 7-8, 21-22, 68 of pdf.) Photocopying charges are generally not recoverable costs in litigation. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 1033.5, subd. (b)(3).) The Court also finds it improper for Receiver to be charging fees for transferring funds to pay itself. Additionally, the Court finds the $223.56 incurred for obtaining a copy of the Court’s order granting Plaintiff’s motion for appointment of receiver is not reasonable, when such a copy could be easily obtained for a nominal fee on the Court’s website. (March 2026 Report, p. 48 of pdf.) 

            Based on the foregoing, the Court finds that the fair value of the services received is $37,153.45. (See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1183, subd. (a).) The Court therefore APPROVES Receiver’s March 2026 report in the amount of $37,153.45. 

CONCLUSION 

The Court APPROVES Receiver’s March 2026 report in the amount of $37,153.45. 

             Receiver is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order.

April 2026 Monthly Accounting of Receivership Income, Expenses, and Interim Fees 

TENTATIVE RULING 

The Court APPROVES Receiver’s April 2026 report in the amount of $23,173.66. 

             Receiver is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order. 

BACKGROUND 

This is a nuisance case. On August 25, 2025, plaintiff City of Glendora (Plaintiff) filed this action against defendants Tong Zhou (Zhou), Ying Xia (Xia) (collectively, Defendants) and Does 1 through 20, alleging causes of action for public nuisance per se, public nuisance, violation of state housing law – receivership, and declaration/injunctive relief. 

On February 18, 2026, the Court approved Plaintiff’s motion for appointment of receiver and appointed California Receivership Group, Inc. (Receiver) as receiver over the subject property. 

On June 1, 2026, Receiver filed the April 2026 monthly accounting of receivership income, expenses, and interim fees. On June 8, 2026, Plaintiff objected to the accounting report. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

(a) Content of reports 

The receiver must provide monthly reports to the parties and, if requested, to nonparty client lien holders. These reports must include: 

(1) A narrative report of events; 

(2) A financial report; and 

(3) A statement of all fees paid to the receiver, employees, and professionals showing: 

(A) Itemized services; 

(B) A breakdown of the services by 1/10 hour increments; 

(C) If the fees are hourly, the hourly fees; and 

(D) If the fees are on another basis, that basis. 

(b) Reports not to be filed 

The monthly reports are not to be filed with the court unless the court so orders. 

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1182.) 

PRELIMINARY ISSUE 

            Financial account information is supposed to be redacted. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 1.201, subd. (a)(2).) Receiver failed to redact a bank account number. (April 2026 Report, p. 42 of pdf.) The Court admonishes Receiver to comply with the California Rules of Court going forward. 

DISCUSSION 

Summary of Arguments 

Receiver’s April 2026 report indicates having incurred $28,551.40 in receivership fees. Receiver states that total unpaid receivership fees and unpaid advances as of this reporting period, including April, are $60,169.15 and $1,860.98, respectively. Receiver sets forth details regarding rehabilitation work performed on the subject property through the month of April 2026. 

            Plaintiff objects to the billing entries the Court found objectionable at the April 27, 2026 hearing, the hours the Receiver’s employees billed for time spent overseeing the occupants’ cleanout of the subject property, and Receiver’s overhead expenses associated with travel for one of its employees who resides in Northern California, including his flight, hotel stay, and car rental. Plaintiff objects to billing entries incurred by 13 employees other than the Receiver that reflect duplication of effort or administrative tasks and contends the receivership estate should not be expected to pay travel time and expenses for an employee who does not reside locally or pay for nearly six hours of travel time. 

            Analysis 

            The Court has reviewed the April 2026 report and finds the $28,551.40 in receivership fees excessive. The Court notes approximately 14 timekeepers involved in this matter. While the Court understands and appreciates that multiple people are necessary for the significant demands involved in rehabilitating a property, 14 people is excessive. Of particular note is the extensive amount of minor billing entries from each of these timekeepers in the amounts of 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 hours throughout the April 2026 report. (See April 2026 Report, pp. 45-76 of pdf.) The Court also notes that many of these charges contain block billing. (Heritage Pac. Fin., LLC v. Monroy (2013) 215 Cal.App.4th 972, 1010, internal citation omitted, “[t]rial courts retain discretion to penalize block billing when the practice prevents them from discerning which tasks are compensable and which are not…”) 

            The Court agrees with Plaintiff that many of the charges in the April 2026 report are for administrative matters, such as internal coordination, recurring meetings, bookkeeping/accounting, and processing credit card charges, among other things. The Court will therefore deduct $4,771.20 as follows:

             The Court further agrees with Plaintiff that charges for Christopher Bolton to travel from Northern California to the subject property, including hotel stay and rental car, were not reasonable charges. May 2026 Monthly Accounting of Receivership Income, Expenses, and Interim Fees 

TENTATIVE RULING 

The Court APPROVES Receiver’s May 2026 report in the amount of $16,902.90. 

             Receiver is ordered to give notice of the Court’s ruling within five calendar days of this order. 

BACKGROUND 

This is a nuisance case. On August 25, 2025, plaintiff City of Glendora (Plaintiff) filed this action against defendants Tong Zhou (Zhou), Ying Xia (Xia) (collectively, Defendants) and Does 1 through 20, alleging causes of action for public nuisance per se, public nuisance, violation of state housing law – receivership, and declaration/injunctive relief. 

On February 18, 2026, the Court approved Plaintiff’s motion for appointment of receiver and appointed California Receivership Group, Inc. (Receiver) as receiver over the subject property. 

On June 29, 2026, Receiver filed the May 2026 monthly accounting of receivership income, expenses, and interim fees. On July 8, 2026, Plaintiff objected to the accounting report. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

(a) Content of reports 

The receiver must provide monthly reports to the parties and, if requested, to nonparty client lien holders. These reports must include: 

(1) A narrative report of events; 

(2) A financial report; and 

(3) A statement of all fees paid to the receiver, employees, and professionals showing: 

(A) Itemized services; 

(B) A breakdown of the services by 1/10 hour increments; 

(C) If the fees are hourly, the hourly fees; and 

(D) If the fees are on another basis, that basis. 

(b) Reports not to be filed 

The monthly reports are not to be filed with the court unless the court so orders. 

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1182.) 

PRELIMINARY ISSUE 

            Financial account information is supposed to be redacted. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 1.201, subd. (a)(2).) Receiver failed to redact a bank account number. (May 2026 Report, p. 4 of pdf.) The Court admonishes Receiver to comply with the California Rules of Court going forward. 

DISCUSSION 

Summary of Arguments 

Receiver’s May 2026 report indicates having incurred $19,607.60 in receivership fees. Receiver states that total unpaid receivership fees and unpaid advances as of this reporting period, including May, are $70,554.75 and $2,083.63, respectively. Receiver sets forth details regarding rehabilitation work performed on the subject property through the month of May 2026. 

Plaintiff objects on the grounds that the May 2026 accounting contains duplicative billing and billing for administrative work that does not advance the receivership or provide a direct benefit to the receivership estate. Plaintiff objects to billing for ordinary administrative and bookkeeping functions that constitute office overhead rather than compensable receivership services. Plaintiff objects to billing for internal management conferences and coordination meetings. Plaintiff also objects on the grounds that Receiver is overstaffing this matter. 

            Analysis 

            The Court has reviewed the May 2026 report and finds the $19,607.60 in receivership fees excessive. The Court notes approximately 14 timekeepers involved in this matter. While the Court understands and appreciates that multiple people are necessary for the significant demands involved in rehabilitating a property, 14 people is excessive. Of particular note is the extensive amount of minor billing entries from each of these timekeepers in the amounts of 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 hours throughout the May 2026 report. (See May 2026 Report, pp. 17-41 of pdf.) The Court also notes that many of these charges contain block billing. (Heritage Pac. Fin., LLC v. Monroy (2013) 215 Cal.App.4th 972, 1010, internal citation omitted, “[t]rial courts retain discretion to penalize block billing when the practice prevents them from discerning which tasks are compensable and which are not…”) 

            The Court also agrees with Plaintiff that charges for internal coordination, recurring meetings, and bookkeeping/accounting should be treated as overhead rather than separate charges billed to the receivership estate. The Court will therefore deduct $2,704.70 in billing as follows:
